answer.rationale: Rollback is contractually excluded because compliance has ruled the security patch must not be reverted, even though memory_b1 shows rollback historically fixed similar write-path error spikes—verifying b1 confirms this precedent doesn't apply under current constraints. Regional failover (b2) and circuit breaking (b4) both risk shedding or rerouting in-flight writes during peak settlement traffic, conflicting with the objective of not losing customer writes. Read replica routing (b5) addresses read load, not the write-path latency degradation described here. Provisioning headroom (b3) previously absorbed a peak-traffic surge without customer impact and is the closest structural analog to current conditions: peak settlement writes plus climbing p99 latency. I verify b3 to confirm the original conditions (surge type, lead time needed, headroom sizing) actually match today's write-path pressure before committing capacity, and verify b1 only to confirm it's the security-patched release being discussed so I don't mistakenly conflate this incident with a simple bad-build scenario. Given verification is limited and this is a live sustained-latency incident at peak load, I'm scaling as a standard experiment rather than broad rollout to avoid overcommitting resources based on a single precedent, while treating the mapping from b3's surge scenario to this write-latency scenario as not fully certain.
